mcqs.question: A team's pipeline automatically builds, tests, and packages every merge into a release-ready artifact, but a human decides when it actually goes to production. What are they practicing?
options: Continuous Deployment — every change ships automatically
Continuous Delivery — always releasable, but a human decides when to release
Continuous Integration only — they don't have any form of CD
Trunk-based development
mcqs.explanation: Continuous Delivery means every passing change is release-ready, with a human or scheduled process choosing the release moment; Continuous Deployment removes that human gate. Since they still have a build/test pipeline producing a real artifact, this is more than plain CI.

mcqs.question: What's the main advantage of blue-green deployment over a rolling deployment, and what does that advantage cost?
options: Blue-green needs less infrastructure, since only one environment ever exists
Blue-green avoids ever needing health checks before serving traffic
Blue-green enables near-instant rollback by flipping the router back to the untouched old environment, at the cost of running two full environments during the switch
Blue-green is always cheaper because it reuses the exact same running instances as rolling
mcqs.explanation: Because the old environment stays fully intact and idle after the switch, rollback is just re-flipping the router — no reverse rollout needed. That speed is bought with roughly double the infrastructure during the switch window, unlike rolling, which reuses existing capacity.

mcqs.question: What makes a traffic split a genuine canary deployment rather than just a slow rolling deployment with extra steps?
options: Sending 50% of production traffic to the new version immediately
Manually eyeballing logs after each stage before deciding to continue
Running the new version on cheaper hardware than the stable version
Automated comparison of the canary's metrics against the baseline, driving the decision to advance or abort each stage
mcqs.explanation: Canary's defining feature is automated metric comparison deciding whether to widen the traffic split or roll back — without it, you just have a manually-gated rollout. A 50% starting split also defeats the purpose of a small, expendable initial exposure.

mcqs.question: Which deployment strategy gives the fastest rollback, and why?
options: Rolling — because it only ever changes one instance at a time
Canary — because only a small percentage of traffic was ever affected
All three roll back at the same speed since they all rely on health checks
Blue-green — rollback is just flipping the router back to the untouched, fully-intact old environment
mcqs.explanation: Rolling requires reversing the rollout batch by batch, which takes real time; canary rollback is fast but still involves shrinking a live split. Blue-green's old environment was never touched, so reverting is an instant router flip — the fastest of the three.

mcqs.question: Why must automated promotion/abort decisions during a rollout not wait for a human to check a dashboard?
options: Because a bad deploy can happen at any time, including when no one is watching, and the pipeline itself must detect and react within the observation window
Because health checks are only a formality and rarely fail in practice
Because dashboards are inherently less reliable than raw log files
Because human review always takes longer than the deployment itself, regardless of the situation
mcqs.explanation: A rollout that starts erroring at 2am needs to be caught and rolled back by the pipeline's own metric thresholds, not left broken until a human notices. Health checks and promotion logic exist precisely because human observation isn't guaranteed to be timely.

mcqs.question: A team has automated rollback logic in its canary pipeline but has never actually triggered a rollback outside of a real incident. What's the risk?
options: None — since the rollback logic runs automatically, it's always guaranteed to work
Automated rollback logic removes any need to ever test it manually
The rollback path may be broken in ways nobody has discovered — a stale config reference or an irreversible migration — and the first real test happens under incident pressure
Rollback speed doesn't matter as long as canary percentages start small
mcqs.explanation: Rollback is a capability like any other code path — untested code paths break. An automated abort trigger that's never fired for real can hide a broken script or an irreversible migration until the exact moment you need it most.
